source.title: Scaling laws for activation steering with Llama 2 models and refusal mechanisms
source.citation: Sheikh Abdur Raheem Ali et al., 2025
source.authors: Sheikh Abdur Raheem Ali; Justin Xu; Ivory Yang; Jasmine Xinze Li; Ayse Arslan; Clark Benham

record.file_problem: The supplied text includes the paper's main sections and references, but refers to an appendix for the refusal dataset that is not included. Figures 3–5 are represented by captions rather than their plotted data.
record.tranche_reason: The study investigates how contrastive activation addition affects refusal answers as Llama 2 model size changes. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss, test predictions from smaller-run loss fits, or examine compute-optimal parameter/token allocation.
record.gate_note: The reported activation-steering results concern induced refusal behavior, not any of the claim versions' loss, compute allocation, architecture-versus-loss, modality, or downstream-predictability measures. The steering results are recorded as related findings with versions ["none"], not as tests of the claim.
record.test_reason: The study measures how well contrastive activation addition steers refusal answers across Llama 2 7B, 13B and 70B. It reports no pretraining loss, no loss extrapolation, no compute allocation, no architecture-versus-loss comparison, no other-modality loss curves, and no downstream predictability from scale or loss. It borrows only the phrase 'scaling laws' and does not cite either original source. Its size trend in steering effectiveness is a different construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors find CAA is most effective at early-mid layers (~0.4 × depth), weakens with model size, and is stronger for negative than positive steering. They caution that results are limited to the refusal topic.
record.recipe_differences: The study sweeps CAA interventions on refusal answer matching across Llama 2 model sizes and layers; it does not use the original studies' held-out-loss scaling or compute-allocation measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported steering outcomes vary with model size, injection layer, and steering direction (positive versus negative).

fits_no_version.finding: Peak CAA refusal-steering effectiveness falls with model size across Llama 2 7B/13B/70B. The authors fit y = 0.081 + 2.4·e^(−0.42x).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation-steering effectiveness for a fixed behaviour decreases with model scale.

fits_no_version.finding: Negative steering (toward non-refusal) is more effective than positive steering at all three sizes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In RLHF chat models, steering away from refusal is easier than steering toward it.

fits_no_version.finding: Peak steering layer is about 0.4 × layer count. The positive/negative peak-layer gap shrinks from 2 layers at 7B to 0 at 70B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The optimal steering layer scales proportionally with depth, and positive and negative peaks converge with size.

record.problems: The supplied text omits the referenced appendix and the plotted values in Figures 3–5. It does not state numerical uncertainty estimates or detailed dataset counts. The text also contains inconsistent venue/year boilerplate: it says accepted by a 2025 workshop and separately includes a Proceedings of ICML 2024 line.

untested.parts: All: no held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
All: no extrapolation of loss fits from small to large runs.
All: no loss comparison across depth/width at fixed parameter count.
All: no power-law loss in other modalities or training regimes.
All: refusal answer-matching is measured only under steering. No unsteered downstream trend versus scale or loss is reported.
All: no exponent fitting of loss or compute-optimal split.

record.verdict_notes: The paper does not cite Kaplan et al. or Hoffmann et al. 'Relation: discusses' is generous: the overlap is only the phrase 'scaling laws' in the title. The record's 'cannot_determine' row states are appropriate given versions ['none']. The text carries both an ICML 2024 proceedings boilerplate line and a 2025 workshop note.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens, or compute.
Whether loss fits on small runs predict loss on much larger runs.
Architecture effects on held-out loss at fixed parameter count.
Power-law loss behavior in other modalities or training regimes.
Predictability of downstream task performance from scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of held-out-loss exponents or compute-optimal allocation on setup or fitting choices.

rows.subject: Llama-2 family (7B, 13B, and 70B)
rows.operation_detail: Compared peak CAA steering effectiveness across model parameter counts.
rows.measure: Peak steering effectiveness as a function of parameter count
rows.note: The paper describes effectiveness as decreasing with model size and gives an exponential fit. This is a fit for steering effectiveness, not held-out loss.
rows.check: Link and state are correct. The fit is exponential, not a power law. The units of x (parameter count) are not stated. With only three model sizes, the fit is weakly constrained.

rows.subject: Llama-2 family (7B, 13B, and 70B)
rows.operation_detail: Compared positive and negative CAA steering on refusal answer matching.
rows.measure: Maximum change in correct refusal behavior
rows.baseline: Unsteered answer-matching performance; value not stated
rows.value: Negative steering was reported as significantly more effective than positive steering across all three model sizes.
rows.note: Aggregate statement across the three models; numerical plotted values are not present in the supplied text.

rows.subject: Llama-2 family (7B, 13B, and 70B)

rows.value: Peak efficacy occurs at approximately 0.4 × total layer count.
rows.note: The paper says this finding may differ for other topics or prompting approaches.
